# Heatwaves and Cold-spells {.unnumbered}

Authors: Nicholas Wu

Detecting, describing and classifying extreme temperature events with a structured, reproducible workflow following the [`heatwaveR`](https://robwschlegel.github.io/heatwaveR/) package R [@Schlegel2018].

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Workshop overview

**By the end of this workshop you will be able to:**

1. Explain how heatwaves and cold-spells are defined, and recognise the common 
   problems that change the number and size of detected events.
2. Detect and describe events in **daily** and **hourly** temperature data with
   the [`heatwaveR`](https://robwschlegel.github.io/heatwaveR/) package
   [@Schlegel2018].
3. Classify event severity and scale the workflow to many locations (gridded
   data).
4. Report the workflow and interpret events in terms of **biological impact**,
   e.g. with thermal-death-time models.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center", comment = "#>")
```

## Background {.unnumbered}

### What is a heatwave? {.unnumbered}

In everyday language a heatwave is "a run of unusually hot days". To compare
events between places, seasons and decades we need a precise, *relative*
definition. In a **relative** definition, "unusually hot" means hot *for that
place and time of year*, so a 25 °C day can be a heatwave in winter but not in
summer.

For the ocean, @Hobday2016 defined a **marine heatwave (MHW)** as a *prolonged
discrete anomalously warm water event* and operationalised it as at least
**5 consecutive days** above a **seasonally varying 90th percentile threshold**,
calculated from a **30-year baseline (climatology) period**, with events
separated by **2 days or fewer joined together** (@fig-hw-metrics). The same
algorithm, with the 10th percentile and temperatures *below* the threshold,
detects **marine cold-spells (MCS)** [@Schlegel2017; @Schlegel2021].
@Hobday2018 then named events by their **category**: how many multiples of the
threshold–climatology difference the peak exceeds (I Moderate, II Strong,
III Severe, IV Extreme).

![Anatomy of a heatwave following @Hobday2016 and @Hobday2018. The climatology (grey) is the seasonal mean and the threshold (green) the seasonally varying 90th percentile of the baseline period. An event needs ≥ 5 days above the threshold; short spikes are ignored and gaps of ≤ 2 days are bridged. Event metrics are measured relative to the climatology, and the category depends on how many multiples of the threshold–climatology difference the temperature reaches.](images/hw_metrics.svg){#fig-hw-metrics fig-alt="Annotated temperature time series showing climatology, threshold, an event shaded by category, duration, maximum intensity, onset and decline rates, and how gaps and short spikes are treated." width="100%"}

For the atmosphere, there is no single universal definition. Definitions use
daily maximum (Tmax), minimum (Tmin) or mean temperature, relative (percentile)
or absolute thresholds, heat-stress indices that combine temperature and
humidity, and minimum durations that are usually **3 days**
[@Perkins2013; @Perkins2015; @Nairn2015]. @Perkins2013 recommended describing
heatwaves with a small set of metrics (number, frequency, duration, amplitude
and magnitude), which maps closely onto the metrics in @fig-hw-metrics.

The table below summarises the main metrics returned by `heatwaveR`:

| Metric | Meaning | Units (daily data) |
|----|----|----|
| `duration` | Days from start to end of the event | days |
| `intensity_max` | Peak temperature anomaly relative to the climatology | °C |
| `intensity_mean` | Mean anomaly over the event | °C |
| `intensity_cumulative` | Sum of daily anomalies (area under the curve) | °C × days |
| `rate_onset`, `rate_decline` | How fast the event developed and decayed | °C day^-1^ |
| `*_relThresh`, `*_abs` | Same intensities relative to the threshold, or as absolute temperatures | °C |

### Why are heatwaves important in thermal ecology? {.unnumbered}

Extreme events, not just gradual warming, drive many of the biggest ecological
responses to climate change [@Harris2018]. Marine heatwaves have become longer
and more frequent over the past century [@Oliver2018], and they cause mass
mortality, range shifts and loss of habitat-forming species [@Smale2019;
@Smith2023]. The 2011 Western Australian MHW, the dataset you will analyse
below, contributed to a regime shift from kelp forests to seaweed turfs
[@Wernberg2016]. On land, heatwaves are projected to become more frequent,
persistent and intense across almost all inhabited regions [@Domeisen2023].

### Why a structured, reproducible workflow? {.unnumbered}

The number, duration and intensity of events you detect depend on many choices:
the dataset, the baseline period, the percentile, the minimum duration, how gaps
and missing data are treated, and whether the time series is detrended. These
choices are often under-reported, so results from different studies are hard to
compare or synthesise [@Hobday2016; @Schlegel2019; @Amaya2023].

A shared algorithm implemented in open code solves much of this.
`heatwaveR` is the R implementation of the Hobday et al. definitions (a faster
successor to the original Python and `RmarineHeatWaves` code), works on air
and water temperatures, on daily and hourly data, and makes every parameter an
explicit, reportable function argument [@Schlegel2018]. Writing the workflow as
code means you can rerun it when new data arrive, apply it identically to
thousands of grid cells, and share it with your paper.

## Common problems {.unnumbered}

| Problem | Effect on detected events | How to handle it |
|----|----|----|
| **Short time series** (< 30 years) | Unstable percentiles; thresholds too low or too high | Use ≥ 30 years where possible; report the baseline; see @Schlegel2019 |
| **Missing data** | Events split into pieces or missed | Report % missing; interpolate short gaps only (`maxPadLength`); see @Schlegel2019 |
| **Long-term trend in the data** | With a fixed baseline, late years are "always in a heatwave" | Decide (and report) fixed vs. shifting baseline or detrending [@Amaya2023] |
| **Choice of baseline period** | Different baselines give different event counts | Use a standard 30-year period (e.g. 1982–2011 for OISST; WMO 1991–2020) and report it |
| **Resolution** (daily vs. hourly; satellite vs. in situ) | Daily means hide extremes that organisms feel | Match the data resolution to the biological question |
| **Definition choices** (percentile, `minDuration`, `maxGap`) | Event number and duration change | Use established defaults (5/2 marine, 3/1 atmospheric) or justify alternatives |
| **Events at the ends of the series** | `rate_onset`/`rate_decline` are `NA`; durations truncated | Interpret edge events with care |
| **Hemisphere and season** | Wrong season labels in `category()` | Set `S = TRUE` for the southern hemisphere |
| **Relative vs. absolute stress** | A "Severe" winter event may be biologically harmless | Combine relative events with absolute, organism-specific thresholds (see Caveats) |

Without a reproducible workflow there are additional problems: thresholds
computed once in a spreadsheet and copied between sites, baseline periods that
silently differ between analyses, missing-data handling that is never
documented, and results that cannot be updated when new data arrive.

## Example Workflow {.unnumbered}

At minimum, your data need:

- a **date** column (class `Date`, "YYYY-MM-DD") for daily data, or a date-time
  column (class `POSIXct`, on the hour) for hourly data, named `t` by default; and
- a **temperature** column, named `temp` by default (other names can be passed
  with the `x` and `y` arguments).

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Run once to install
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "heatwaveR", "maps"))
```

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and plotting
library(heatwaveR) # heatwave and cold-spell detection
```

The workflow has three core steps: build a climatology and
threshold with `ts2clm()`, detect events with `detect_event()`, and classify them
with `category()`.

`heatwaveR` comes with four example datasets:

| Dataset | Content | Period |
|----|----|----|
| `sst_WA` | Daily sea surface temperature (SST), Western Australia | 1982–2022 |
| `sst_NW_Atl` | Daily SST, Northwest Atlantic | 1982–2022 |
| `sst_Med` | Daily SST, Mediterranean | 1982–2022 |
| `Algiers` | Daily air Tmax and Tmin, Algiers (Algeria) | 1961–2005 |

::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills}

# Daily data {.unnumbered}

## Import {.unnumbered}

The example data are already loaded with the package. With your own data, the
pattern is: read, fix column types, and aggregate to the resolution you need.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Example only: a logger file with a date-time column and temperature
my_daily <- read_csv("data/my_logger.csv") |>
  mutate(date_time = ymd_hms(date_time)) |>
  group_by(t = as_date(date_time)) |>
  summarise(temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r}
sst_WA
```

## Quality check {.unnumbered}

Before detecting anything, check that the record is long enough, complete,
regular and free of duplicates, and look at it.

```{r}
check_series <- function(df) {
  df |>
    summarise(start      = min(t),
              end        = max(t),
              years      = round(as.numeric(end - start) / 365.25, 1),
              n_days     = n(),
              n_expected = as.numeric(end - start) + 1,
              n_missing  = sum(is.na(temp)) + (n_expected - n_days),
              n_dup      = sum(duplicated(t)))
}

check_series(sst_WA)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sst-wa
#| fig-cap: "Daily SST off Western Australia (grey) with annual means (black) and a linear trend (red)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| message: false
wa_annual <- sst_WA |>
  group_by(year = year(t)) |>
  summarise(temp = mean(temp))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = sst_WA, aes(x = t, y = temp), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = wa_annual, aes(x = as.Date(paste0(year, "-07-01")), y = temp)) +
  geom_smooth(data = wa_annual, aes(x = as.Date(paste0(year, "-07-01")), y = temp),
              method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#e12744") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SST (°C)") +
  theme_linedraw()
```

The record is 41 years long with no gaps, which is ideal. Note the warming
trend: with a fixed 1982–2011 baseline, warmer recent years will produce more
events. This is not an error, but it is a decision to report (see Caveats).

## Detect events {.unnumbered}

### Marine heatwaves {.unnumbered}

`ts2clm()` calculates, for each day of the year, the climatological mean (`seas`)
and the 90th percentile threshold (`thresh`) from the baseline period, pooling
values within ±5 days (`windowHalfWidth`) and smoothing with a 31-day moving
average (`smoothPercentileWidth`). `detect_event()` then finds runs of days
above the threshold.

```{r}
ts_WA  <- ts2clm(sst_WA, climatologyPeriod = c("1982-01-01", "2011-12-31"))
mhw_WA <- detect_event(ts_WA)   # defaults: minDuration = 5, maxGap = 2

ts_WA |> head()
```

`detect_event()` returns a list with a `climatology` data frame (the daily data
with the threshold and event flags) and an `event` data frame (one row per event).

```{r}
mhw_WA$event |>
  select(event_no, duration, date_start, date_peak,
         intensity_max, intensity_cumulative) |>
  arrange(desc(intensity_max)) |>
  head(5)
```

The largest event is the 2011 "Ningaloo Niño" heatwave. `event_line()` and
`lolli_plot()` give quick visual summaries.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wa-event
#| fig-cap: "The 2011 marine heatwave off Western Australia drawn with `event_line()`."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false
event_line(mhw_WA, spread = 180, metric = intensity_max,
           start_date = "1982-01-01", end_date = "2014-12-31") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-wa-line
#| fig-cap: "All detected marine heatwave events off Western Australia drawn with `lolli_plot()`."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| warning: false
lolli_plot(mhw_WA, metric = intensity_max)
```

For full control, `geom_flame()` adds the event "flames" to any `ggplot`. In **Fig. 5**,
the timespan is from the 11th November 2010 to 32st May 2011.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wa-flame
#| fig-cap: "The 2011 Western Australian marine heatwave drawn with `geom_flame().`"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
mhw_WA$climatology |>
  filter(t >= as.Date("2010-11-01"), t <= as.Date("2011-05-31")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = t)) +
  geom_flame(aes(y = temp, y2 = thresh), fill = "#e12744") +
  geom_line(aes(y = temp), colour = "black") +
  geom_line(aes(y = seas), colour = "grey50", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = thresh), colour = "forestgreen", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SST (°C)") +
  theme_linedraw()
```

### Marine cold-spells {.unnumbered}

Cold-spells use the **10th** percentile threshold and `coldSpells = TRUE`.

```{r}
ts_WA_10 <- ts2clm(sst_WA, climatologyPeriod = c("1982-01-01", "2011-12-31"),
                   pctile = 10)
mcs_WA   <- detect_event(ts_WA_10, coldSpells = TRUE)

mcs_WA$event |>
  select(event_no, duration, date_start, date_peak,
         intensity_max, intensity_cumulative) |>
  arrange(intensity_cumulative) |>
  head(5)
```

Intensities of cold-spells are negative (below the climatology).

### Atmospheric heatwaves and cold-spells {.unnumbered}

For air temperature we follow the common atmospheric convention of at least
**3 consecutive days** above the 90th percentile of **Tmax** (heatwaves) or
below the 10th percentile of **Tmin** (cold-spells) [@Perkins2013], and join
gaps of 1 day (the atmospheric default suggested in the `heatwaveR`
documentation). Because the column is not called `temp`, tell both functions
which column to use with `y`.

```{r}
ts_alg_tmax <- ts2clm(Algiers, y = tMax,
                      climatologyPeriod = c("1961-01-01", "1990-12-31"))
hw_alg <- detect_event(ts_alg_tmax, y = tMax, minDuration = 3, maxGap = 1)

ts_alg_tmin <- ts2clm(Algiers, y = tMin, pctile = 10,
                      climatologyPeriod = c("1961-01-01", "1990-12-31"))
cs_alg <- detect_event(ts_alg_tmin, y = tMin, coldSpells = TRUE,
                       minDuration = 3, maxGap = 1)

bind_rows(heatwave  = hw_alg$event,
          coldspell = cs_alg$event, .id = "type") |>
  group_by(type) |>
  summarise(n_events      = n(),
            mean_duration = mean(duration),
            max_intensity = max(abs(intensity_max)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-algiers-lolli
#| fig-cap: "Atmospheric heatwaves in Algiers (Tmax)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| warning: false
lolli_plot(hw_alg, metric = intensity_max)
```

## Classify severity {.unnumbered}

`category()` assigns each event a Hobday et al. (2018) category and season.
Western Australia is in the southern hemisphere, so set `S = TRUE`.

```{r}
mhw_cat_WA <- category(mhw_WA, S = TRUE, name = "WA")
mhw_cat_WA |> head()

mhw_cat_WA |> count(category)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-wa-category
#| fig-cap: "Categories of the 2011 Western Australian marine heatwave."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| warning: false
event_line(mhw_WA, spread = 100, start_date = "2010-11-01",
           end_date = "2011-06-30", category = TRUE) 
```

The same function classifies cold-spells; it detects that it has been given
cold-spells.

```{r}
mcs_cat_WA <- category(mcs_WA, S = TRUE, name = "WA")
mcs_cat_WA |> count(category)
```

### Absolute thresholds with `exceedance()` {.unnumbered}

Sometimes the relevant question is not "unusually hot for this place?" but "above
a temperature that harms my organism?". `exceedance()` detects runs above (or,
with `below = TRUE`, below) a fixed threshold.

```{r}
exc_26 <- exceedance(sst_WA, threshold = 26, minDuration = 5, maxGap = 2)

exc_26$exceedance |>
  select(exceedance_no, date_start, duration, intensity_max) |>
  arrange(desc(duration)) |>
  head(5)
```


# Hourly data {.unnumbered}

Daily means smooth out the afternoon peaks and night-time lows that organisms
actually experience. `heatwaveR` (from v0.5.4) also accepts **hourly** data, with
a `POSIXct` time column on exact hours. All window and duration arguments are
then in **hours**.

`heatwaveR` does not include an hourly dataset, so we reconstruct one from the
daily Algiers Tmax and Tmin with a simple sine-shaped diurnal cycle (maximum at
15:00, minimum at 03:00). Real diurnal cycles are asymmetric, so this is for
teaching only; with your own logger data you would skip this step.

## Import {.unnumbered}

```{r}
# Hourly code is time-zone sensitive: work in UTC to avoid daylight saving shifts
Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")

alg_hourly <- Algiers |>
  filter(t >= as.Date("1971-01-01")) |>          # 35 years keeps run time short
  uncount(24, .id = "hour") |>
  mutate(hour = hour - 1,
         temp = (tMax + tMin) / 2 +
                (tMax - tMin) / 2 * cos(2 * pi * (hour - 15) / 24),
         t    = as.POSIXct(t, tz = "UTC") + hour * 3600) |>
  select(t, temp) |>
  arrange(t)

alg_hourly |> head()
```

## Quality check {.unnumbered}

```{r}
alg_hourly |>
  summarise(start        = min(t),
            end          = max(t),
            n_hours      = n(),
            n_expected   = as.numeric(difftime(end, start, units = "hours")) + 1,
            off_the_hour = sum(minute(t) != 0 | second(t) != 0),
            n_missing    = sum(is.na(temp)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-hourly-check
#| fig-cap: "Reconstructed hourly air temperature in Algiers for July 2003 (line) with daily Tmax and Tmin (points)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
alg_hourly |>
  filter(t >= as.POSIXct("2003-07-01", tz = "UTC"),
         t <  as.POSIXct("2003-08-01", tz = "UTC")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = t, y = temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = Algiers |>
               filter(t >= as.Date("2003-07-01"), t < as.Date("2003-08-01")) |>
               pivot_longer(c(tMax, tMin), values_to = "temp") |>
               mutate(t = as.POSIXct(t, tz = "UTC") + if_else(name == "tMax", 15, 3) * 3600),
             aes(colour = name)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(tMax = "#e12744", tMin = "#2b6cb0")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Air temperature (°C)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_linedraw()
```

## Detect events {.unnumbered}

Scale every time-based argument from days to hours: a ±5-day window becomes
`windowHalfWidth = 5 * 24`, the 31-day smoothing becomes
`smoothPercentileWidth = 31 * 24`, and so on. Here we require at least 3 days
(72 h) above the hour-of-year 90th percentile and allow gaps of up to 12 h (e.g.
a slightly cooler night) to be joined. These are choices you must report.

```{r}
ts_alg_h <- ts2clm(alg_hourly,
                   climatologyPeriod     = c("1971-01-01", "2000-12-31"),
                   windowHalfWidth       = 5 * 24,
                   smoothPercentileWidth = 31 * 24)

hw_alg_h <- detect_event(ts_alg_h, minDuration = 3 * 24, maxGap = 12)

hw_alg_h$event |>
  select(event_no, date_start, date_peak, duration,
         intensity_max, intensity_cumulative) |>
  arrange(desc(intensity_max)) |>
  head(5)
```

Durations are in hours and cumulative intensity in °C × hours.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hourly-event
#| fig-cap: "The most intense hourly heatwave in the reconstructed Algiers record. Red shading shows hours above the hour-of-year threshold (green)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
top_h <- hw_alg_h$event |> slice_max(intensity_max, n = 1)

hw_alg_h$climatology |>
  filter(t >= top_h$date_start - 3 * 86400,
         t <= top_h$date_end   + 3 * 86400) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = t)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = thresh, ymax = pmax(temp, thresh)),
              fill = "#e12744", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = seas), colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = thresh), colour = "forestgreen", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = temp)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Air temperature (°C)") +
  theme_linedraw()
```

Hourly cold-spells work the same way:

```{r}
ts_alg_h10 <- ts2clm(alg_hourly,
                     climatologyPeriod     = c("1971-01-01", "2000-12-31"),
                     windowHalfWidth       = 5 * 24,
                     smoothPercentileWidth = 31 * 24,
                     pctile = 10)

cs_alg_h <- detect_event(ts_alg_h10, coldSpells = TRUE,
                         minDuration = 3 * 24, maxGap = 12)

nrow(cs_alg_h$event)
```


# Gridded data {.unnumbered}

Gridded products such as NOAA OISST give one time series per pixel. Detecting
events on a grid is the same workflow applied to each pixel with
`group_by()` + `group_modify()`. Here the three SST datasets play the role of
three pixels.

```{r}
sites <- bind_rows(
  sst_WA     |> mutate(site = "WA",     lon = 112.625, lat = -29.375),
  sst_NW_Atl |> mutate(site = "NW_Atl", lon = -66.875, lat =  43.125),
  sst_Med    |> mutate(site = "Med",    lon =   9.125, lat =  43.625)
)

# One function per pixel: climatology -> events -> categories
event_cat <- function(df, key) {
  df |>
    ts2clm(climatologyPeriod = c("1982-01-01", "2011-12-31")) |>
    detect_event() |>
    category(S = key$lat < 0, name = key$site)
}

mhw_sites <- sites |>
  group_by(site, lon, lat) |>
  group_modify(\(df, key) event_cat(df, key)) |>
  ungroup()

mhw_sites |> count(site, category)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sites-map
#| fig-cap: "Total marine heatwave days (1982–2022) at the three example sites."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
site_summary <- mhw_sites |>
  group_by(site, lon, lat) |>
  summarise(n_events = n(), mhw_days = sum(duration), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(site_summary, aes(x = lon, y = lat)) +
  annotation_borders("world", fill = "grey85", colour = NA) +
  geom_point(aes(size = mhw_days), colour = "#e12744") +
  geom_text(aes(label = site), nudge_y = 9) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-100, 160), ylim = c(-50, 70)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, size = "MHW days") +
  theme_linedraw()
```

Trends in event frequency are commonly tested per pixel with a Poisson GLM of
annual counts:

```{r}
mhw_counts <- mhw_sites |>
  count(site, year = year(peak_date)) |>
  complete(site, year = 1982:2022, fill = list(n = 0))

mhw_counts |>
  nest(data = -site) |>
  mutate(fit = map(data, \(d) glm(n ~ year, family = poisson, data = d)),
         tidy = map(fit, broom::tidy)) |>
  unnest(tidy) |>
  filter(term == "year") |>
  transmute(site,
            change_per_decade = exp(estimate * 10),  # multiplicative change
            p.value)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Working with real gridded data (OISST)

For real grids, download a subset of NOAA OISST with `rerddap`, then apply the
same `group_by(lon, lat)` + `group_modify()` code. Large grids are best split
into longitude slices and processed in parallel, or handled with the companion
package [`heatwave3`](https://robwschlegel.github.io/heatwave3/), which applies
`heatwaveR` directly to NetCDF files. See the heatwaveR vignettes on
[OISST preparation](https://robwschlegel.github.io/heatwaveR/articles/OISST_preparation.html)
and [gridded event detection](https://robwschlegel.github.io/heatwaveR/articles/gridded_event_detection.html).

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Not run: downloads ~1 year of OISST for a small box off southwest Australia
library(rerddap)

oisst <- griddap(datasetx  = "ncdcOisst21Agg_LonPM180",
                 url       = "https://coastwatch.pfeg.noaa.gov/erddap/",
                 time      = c("2011-01-01", "2011-12-31"),
                 zlev      = c(0, 0),
                 latitude  = c(-32, -28),
                 longitude = c(112, 115),
                 fields    = "sst")$data |>
  mutate(t = as.Date(str_remove(time, "T12:00:00Z"))) |>
  select(lon = longitude, lat = latitude, t, temp = sst) |>
  drop_na()

# Note: event detection needs the full multi-decade record for each pixel,
# so download 1982-present in chunks of < 9 years before running ts2clm().
```
:::

## Activity 1: Another ocean

Detect marine heatwaves in `sst_NW_Atl` (Northwest Atlantic) with a 1982–2011
baseline. (a) How many events are there? (b) Which event had the largest
**cumulative** intensity, and when did it peak? (c) Classify the events; note
this site is in the **northern** hemisphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 1

```{r}
mhw_NWA <- sst_NW_Atl |>
  ts2clm(climatologyPeriod = c("1982-01-01", "2011-12-31")) |>
  detect_event()

nrow(mhw_NWA$event)

mhw_NWA$event |>
  slice_max(intensity_cumulative, n = 1) |>
  select(event_no, date_start, date_peak, duration,
         intensity_max, intensity_cumulative)

category(mhw_NWA, S = FALSE, name = "NW_Atl") |>
  count(category)
```

There are `r nrow(mhw_NWA$event)` events. The largest by cumulative intensity
peaked on
`r mhw_NWA$event |> slice_max(intensity_cumulative, n = 1) |> pull(date_peak)`.
Using `S = FALSE` is essential so that the season labels are correct.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 2: The baseline matters

Repeat the Western Australia detection with a later baseline,
1992-01-01 to 2021-12-31. How many events are detected with each baseline, and
how many events start after 2011? Why do the numbers differ?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 2

```{r}
mhw_WA_late <- sst_WA |>
  ts2clm(climatologyPeriod = c("1992-01-01", "2021-12-31")) |>
  detect_event()

baseline_comp <- bind_rows(
  `1982-2011` = mhw_WA$event,
  `1992-2021` = mhw_WA_late$event,
  .id = "baseline") |>
  group_by(baseline) |>
  summarise(n_events      = n(),
            n_after_2011  = sum(date_start > as.Date("2011-12-31")),
            total_days    = sum(duration))
baseline_comp
```

The later baseline includes warmer years, so the threshold is higher and fewer
events are detected, especially in recent years. Neither is "wrong": a fixed
early baseline measures change relative to a historical state (relevant for
organisms that cannot keep up with warming), while a shifting or detrended
baseline isolates short-term variability [@Amaya2023]. You must report which you
used.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 3: Missing data

Real records have gaps. Set the WA temperatures between 2011-02-10 and
2011-02-20 to `NA` and rerun the detection (a) without interpolation and
(b) with `maxPadLength = 3` and (c) `maxPadLength = 11` in `ts2clm()`. What
happens to the 2011 event?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 3

```{r}
sst_WA_gap <- sst_WA |>
  mutate(temp = if_else(between(t, as.Date("2011-02-10"), as.Date("2011-02-20")),
                        NA_real_, temp))

detect_2011 <- function(pad) {
  sst_WA_gap |>
    ts2clm(climatologyPeriod = c("1982-01-01", "2011-12-31"),
           maxPadLength = pad) |>
    detect_event() |>
    pluck("event") |>
    filter(date_start >= as.Date("2010-12-01"),
           date_start <= as.Date("2011-04-30")) |>
    select(date_start, date_end, duration, intensity_max, intensity_cumulative)
}

detect_2011(FALSE)  # no interpolation
detect_2011(3)      # interpolate gaps up to 3 days only
detect_2011(11)     # interpolate the whole 11-day gap
```

Without interpolation, the 11-day gap is longer than `maxGap`, so the single
105-day event is split into separate events and its duration and cumulative
intensity are underestimated. A `maxPadLength` shorter than the gap does not fill
it. Interpolating the whole gap restores one event, but the interpolated values
are a guess: a straight line from 25.4 to 27.4 °C that misses the real
mid-February warming (up to 27.6 °C), so intensity metrics are still slightly
biased. Report how much data were missing and how gaps were treated
[@Schlegel2019].
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 4: Atmospheric definitions

Using `Algiers`, compare the heatwaves detected with the atmospheric convention
(`minDuration = 3`, `maxGap = 1`) and the marine convention (`minDuration = 5`,
`maxGap = 2`) on Tmax. How many events and heatwave days does each give? Which
year had the most heatwave days under the atmospheric convention?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 4

```{r}
hw_alg_marine <- detect_event(ts_alg_tmax, y = tMax, minDuration = 5, maxGap = 2)

bind_rows(`3 d / gap 1` = hw_alg$event,
          `5 d / gap 2` = hw_alg_marine$event, .id = "definition") |>
  group_by(definition) |>
  summarise(n_events = n(), heatwave_days = sum(duration))

hw_alg$event |>
  group_by(year = year(date_start)) |>
  summarise(heatwave_days = sum(duration)) |>
  slice_max(heatwave_days, n = 1)
```

The shorter minimum duration detects many more, shorter events. Neither choice
is universally correct, which is why the definition must always be reported
alongside the results [@Perkins2013].
:::

# Hourly data {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 5: How long is "prolonged"?

Rerun the hourly heatwave detection with `minDuration = 24` (1 day) and with
`minDuration = 5 * 24` (5 days), keeping `maxGap = 12`. How do the number of
events and their mean duration change? Which definition would you choose to
study heat stress in a small, short-lived insect, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 5

```{r}
tibble(min_hours = c(24, 72, 120)) |>
  mutate(events = map(min_hours, \(m) {
    detect_event(ts_alg_h, minDuration = m, maxGap = 12)$event
  })) |>
  mutate(n_events          = map_int(events, nrow),
         mean_duration_h   = map_dbl(events, \(e) mean(e$duration)),
         total_event_hours = map_dbl(events, \(e) sum(e$duration))) |>
  select(-events)
```

Shorter minimum durations detect many more, shorter events. For a small,
short-lived ectotherm, a day or even a few hours of extreme heat can be
damaging, so a 24-h (or shorter) definition, or an absolute
organism-specific threshold with `exceedance()`, may be more relevant than a
5-day definition designed for ocean temperatures.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 6: Daily vs. hourly

Do the daily (Tmax, 3-day) and hourly heatwaves identify the same periods? For
each daily Tmax heatwave in 1971–2005, check whether any hourly heatwave
overlaps it. What proportion of daily events have an hourly counterpart?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 6

```{r}
daily_ev  <- hw_alg$event |>
  filter(date_start >= as.Date("1971-01-01")) |>
  select(event_no, date_start, date_end)

hourly_ev <- hw_alg_h$event |>
  transmute(h_start = as_date(date_start), h_end = as_date(date_end))

overlap <- daily_ev |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(has_hourly = any(hourly_ev$h_start <= date_end &
                            hourly_ev$h_end >= date_start)) |>
  ungroup()

overlap |> summarise(n_daily = n(), prop_with_hourly = mean(has_hourly))
```

Many but not all daily events have an hourly counterpart. The two approaches use
different thresholds (daily Tmax vs. each hour of the day) and the hourly
definition needs nights to stay warm too. They answer different questions,
so choose the resolution that matches the process you study.
:::

# Gridded data {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 7: Compare the "pixels"

Using `mhw_sites`, which site has (a) the most events, (b) the longest single
event, and (c) the highest proportion of its events in category II or above?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 7

```{r}
mhw_sites |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(n_events        = n(),
            longest_days    = max(duration),
            prop_strong_plus = mean(category != "I Moderate"))
```

Each site has its own climatology, so these are comparisons of *relative*
extremes; a Category II event in the Mediterranean and in Western Australia can
involve very different absolute temperatures.
:::

::: 

# Reporting the Workflow {.unnumbered}

Because the definition determines the result, report every parameter needed to
reproduce the detection:

| Item | Example |
|----|----|
| Data source, resolution and processing | NOAA OISST v2.1, 0.25°, daily; or logger model, depth, sampling interval, aggregation to daily mean |
| Record length and missing data | 1982–2022; 0% missing; gaps ≤ 2 days linearly interpolated (`maxPadLength = 2`) |
| Baseline (climatology) period | 1982-01-01 to 2011-12-31; fixed or shifting; detrended or not |
| Threshold | 90th (heatwaves) / 10th (cold-spells) percentile; or absolute value with `exceedance()` |
| Climatology settings | `windowHalfWidth = 5`, `smoothPercentileWidth = 31` (in hours × 24 for hourly data) |
| Event definition | `minDuration = 5`, `maxGap = 2` (marine) or 3 and 1 (atmospheric) |
| Categories | Hobday et al. (2018), `S = TRUE/FALSE` |
| Software | R and `heatwaveR` versions; cite @Schlegel2018, @Hobday2016, @Hobday2018 |
| Code and outputs | Script, event table and climatology in a public repository |

```{r}
#| eval: false
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(mhw_WA$event, "output/mhw_WA_events.csv")
write_csv(mhw_cat_WA,   "output/mhw_WA_categories.csv")
sessionInfo()
citation("heatwaveR")
```

As with any analysis, the methods text can be generated from the objects
themselves:

> Marine heatwaves were detected in daily SST (1982–2022) with `heatwaveR`
> v`r packageVersion("heatwaveR")` [@Schlegel2018], following @Hobday2016:
> periods of ≥ 5 days above the seasonally varying 90th percentile of a
> 1982–2011 climatology, with gaps of ≤ 2 days joined. We detected
> `r nrow(mhw_WA$event)` events, categorised following @Hobday2018.

# Caveats {.unnumbered}

A heatwave definition describes the **environment**, not the **organism**.
Translating events into biological impact needs care.

- **Relative ≠ harmful.** Percentile thresholds and categories measure how
  unusual a temperature is for that place and season, not whether it exceeds an
  organism's tolerance. A Severe winter event may be harmless and a Moderate
  summer event lethal [@Smith2023].
- **Environment ≠ body temperature.** Air or satellite SST rarely equals the
  body temperature of an organism in a burrow, under a rock, in the intertidal
  or at depth. Microclimate and biophysical models help bridge this gap
  [@Kearney2009; @Sinclair2016].
- **Resolution matters.** Daily means hide the hours of peak heat; tolerance is
  non-linear, so averaging underestimates damage (@fig-tdt-concept).
- **Intensity and duration interact.** Thermal tolerance is a function of both
  temperature and exposure time: the **thermal death time (TDT)** curve
  [@Rezende2014; @Jorgensen2019]. Short, intense events and long, moderate
  events can be equally damaging.
- **Damage accumulates (and sometimes repairs).** Injury can be summed across
  a fluctuating temperature trace by integrating the rate of injury
  ($1/\text{LT}(T)$) over time [@Jorgensen2021; @Rezende2020]. Below a critical
  temperature ($T_c$) damage may not accumulate and repair can occur
  [@Orsted2022]. Acclimation, hardening, life stage and behaviour all modify
  the outcome.
- **Sub-lethal effects** (on growth, reproduction and performance) can occur
  well below lethal limits and over longer timescales [@Harris2018].
- **Small warming, big effects.** Because heat-failure rates rise exponentially
  with temperature, modest increases in peak temperatures can greatly increase
  the frequency of heat failure [@Jorgensen2022].
- **Baselines for biology.** For organisms that cannot acclimate or adapt as
  fast as the climate warms, a fixed historical baseline may better represent
  stress than a shifting one [@Amaya2023].

![The thermal death time (TDT) framework with hypothetical parameters. (a) Survival time declines log-linearly with temperature above a critical temperature $T_c$; $z$ is the temperature increase that reduces survival time ten-fold. (b) The same three days at hourly and daily-mean resolution. (c) Injury, accumulated as $\sum \Delta t/\text{LT}(T)$, is substantial from the hourly trace but almost zero from the daily mean.](images/hw_tdt_concept.svg){#fig-tdt-concept fig-alt="Three panels: a TDT line of log survival time against temperature, hourly vs daily mean temperature traces, and accumulated injury curves." width="100%"}

The TDT model is

$$
\log_{10}\text{LT}(T) = \frac{CT_{\max,1h} - T}{z},
\qquad
\text{injury} = \sum_{T_i \ge T_c} \frac{\Delta t}{\text{LT}(T_i)}
$$

where LT is the time (h) to 50% mortality at temperature $T$, $CT_{\max,1h}$ is
the temperature giving LT = 1 h, and $z$ is the thermal sensitivity
[@Rezende2014; @Jorgensen2021]. An accumulated injury of 1 (100%) predicts 50%
mortality.

```{r}
# Injury rate (per hour) for a temperature, given TDT parameters
injury_rate <- function(temp, ctmax_1h, z, t_c) {
  if_else(temp >= t_c, 10^((temp - ctmax_1h) / z), 0)
}
```

## Activities: biological impact {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 8: Does category predict impact?

Assume a hypothetical temperate marine ectotherm off Western Australia with
$CT_{\max,1h}$ = 36.6 °C, $z$ = 3.7 °C and $T_c$ = 24 °C. Using the daily SST in
`mhw_WA$climatology`, calculate the accumulated injury during each heatwave
(each day contributes 24 h). Join the result to the categories in `mhw_cat_WA`.
(a) Which events are predicted to cause ≥ 50% mortality (injury ≥ 1)?
(b) Does category predict injury?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 8

```{r}
mhw_injury <- mhw_WA$climatology |>
  filter(!is.na(event_no)) |>
  group_by(event_no) |>
  summarise(peak_temp = max(temp),
            injury    = sum(24 * injury_rate(temp, ctmax_1h = 36.6, z = 3.7,
                                             t_c = 24))) |>
  left_join(mhw_cat_WA |> select(event_no, event_name, category, duration),
            by = "event_no")

mhw_injury |>
  filter(injury >= 1) |>
  arrange(desc(injury))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-injury-category
#| fig-cap: "Accumulated injury of a hypothetical ectotherm during each Western Australian marine heatwave, by category. The dashed line marks 50% predicted mortality."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(mhw_injury, aes(x = category, y = injury * 100)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#e12744") +
  geom_jitter(aes(size = duration, colour = peak_temp), width = 0.15, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "inferno", end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Hobday et al. (2018) category", y = "Accumulated injury (%)",
       size = "Duration (days)", colour = "Peak SST (°C)") +
  theme_linedraw()
```

The Extreme 2011 event stands out, but some lower-category events also
accumulate substantial injury because they were long or occurred in the warm
season (with these parameters, a Strong event in 2012 accumulates more injury
than the Severe event in 2008), while winter events accumulate none because
the water stayed below $T_c$.
Category describes how unusual an event is; injury depends on **absolute**
temperature and **duration** relative to the organism's tolerance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 9: Resolution and averaging

For a hypothetical lizard with $CT_{\max,1h}$ = 45 °C, $z$ = 4 °C and
$T_c$ = 36 °C, calculate the injury accumulated in 2003 in Algiers from
(a) the hourly air temperatures (`alg_hourly`), (b) the daily mean
((Tmax + Tmin)/2, applied for 24 h), and (c) the daily maximum (applied for 24 h).
Which is closest to the hourly estimate, and why do the others fail? What other
caveats apply to using air temperature for a lizard?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 9

```{r}
lizard <- list(ctmax_1h = 45, z = 4, t_c = 36)

hourly_2003 <- alg_hourly |>
  filter(year(t) == 2003) |>
  summarise(injury = sum(injury_rate(temp, lizard$ctmax_1h, lizard$z, lizard$t_c)))

daily_2003 <- Algiers |>
  filter(year(t) == 2003) |>
  summarise(
    injury_mean = sum(24 * injury_rate((tMax + tMin) / 2,
                                       lizard$ctmax_1h, lizard$z, lizard$t_c)),
    injury_max  = sum(24 * injury_rate(tMax,
                                       lizard$ctmax_1h, lizard$z, lizard$t_c)))

tibble(resolution = c("hourly", "daily mean", "daily max"),
       injury_pct = 100 * c(hourly_2003$injury,
                            daily_2003$injury_mean,
                            daily_2003$injury_max))
```

The daily mean almost never exceeds $T_c$, so it predicts little or no injury
(because injury rises exponentially with temperature, averaging always
underestimates it). Applying the daily maximum for 24 h assumes the peak lasts
all day and grossly overestimates injury. Only the hourly trace captures the
time spent near the peak. **Further caveats**: lizards thermoregulate behaviourally
and their body temperatures differ from shaded air temperature; the TDT
parameters here are hypothetical; the model ignores repair, acclimation and
hardening; and our hourly series is itself reconstructed from Tmax and Tmin
[@Kearney2009; @Sinclair2016; @Orsted2022].
:::
